question: In early December 2024, the President of the Commission and Mercosur leaders announced that negotiations on the EU-Mercosur partnership agreement had concluded. The Commission described the agreement as ‘groundbreaking’, while President Von der Leyen responded to farmers’ concerns by stating that the ‘agreement includes robust safeguards to protect your livelihoods’.

However, the Commission’s reasoning is selective and the end of negotiations is just the first step towards the agreement potentially being concluded. I would like to draw your attention to the many dangers that the President has seemingly ignored and which are causing concern among EU farmers and are the basis of my objection to the agreement.

Removing EU duties and introducing high tariff quotas runs the risk of EU agricultural products being crowded out by cheaper Mercosur products. Mercosur agricultural production does not take place under conditions that meet EU standards, raising the question of fair competition.

Furthermore, the safeguard mechanisms in the agreement are not adapted to the specific features of the agricultural market, which could make it harder to implement them in the event of excessive imports. Unfortunately, Brussels remains powerless and has been unable to enforce the provisions of already ratified agreements, such as the PDCA with Cuba that has been breached by the regime in Havana.
I question whether the EU has learnt any lessons from the controversial and complex China-EU investment agreement (CAI) that President von der Leyen and Chancellor Merkel pushed for. 1.
Why has the Commission not taken these concerns into account, putting German industrial interests ahead of the future of European farming?
Given the controversy and protests, will the principle of unanimity for concluding the agreement and the requirement for national parliaments to approve it be upheld?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.3.2025) The EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA) is economically and geo-strategically important. It will strengthen strategic cooperation between like-minded partners that share similar values. The EMPA offers export opportunities for several EU agri-food products that will benefit from reduced tariffs in Mercosur countries (e.g.

wines, spirits, confectionary, dairy and olive oil), as well as the protection of EU Geographical Indications in a market of 280 million consumers. For EU sensitive agricultural sectors, trade preferences granted under the EMPA are limited through tariff quotas. Bilateral safeguards can be triggered to protect a specific agricultural sector, including where market access has been limited by tariff quotas.

This would protect farmers in case increased imports from Mercosur cause, or threaten to cause, serious injury to the relevant EU sectors. The Commission will monitor agricultural market developments closely.

For the unlikely event that – despite all precautions – the agricultural market situation in Europe were to be negatively impacted due to the agreement, the Commission announced to set-up a reserve worth at least EUR 1 billion to address possible disturbances in agricultural sectors. After its translation and legal revision, the Commission will present a proposal for signature and conclusion of the EMPA.

In that context, the Commission will present its proposal for the legal basis and architecture of the deal. Any proposed legal architecture will safeguard competences of the EU co-legislators and Member States and their national parliaments, in accordance with the Treaties.
